catalog_quote: [p. 56] It has a system of contrastive tone and contrastive placement of stress. There is also contrast between syllables with single vowels versus syllables with clusters of vowels. There are four contrastive syllable types: CV, CVV, CVC, and CVVC. In words of more than one syllable, syllables with vowel clusters are usually stressed, but vowel clusters do occur in more than one syllable of a few words. The tones which contrast are: high, low, upglide and downglide. Only high and low tones occur on nonstressed syllables. For the most part, stress occurs on the next to the last syllable of a word, but because it does not always occur in that environment, there is contrastive placement of stress. [p. 59] 3. STRESS. sweep_summary: Cerma (cerm1238) is not in the catalog. The single stress-titled item, Hürlimann & Pike 1985 (JWAL 15(2): 56-60), was already held by the project from the earlier download (open JWAL scan, scanned) and was re-read against the page images: it states that stress is for the most part penultimate but placement is contrastive (final, antepenultimate and double-stress words with minimal pairs), and that only stressed syllables carry the glide tones. Two further first-hand phonologies held by the project were checked: Lauber 2006 (SIL ms., 50 pp.) describes a two-tone system and is silent on stress; Prost 1964 (IFAN, phonology excerpt) presupposes stressed vs unstressed vowels in a gemination rule but gives no placement statement. The Glottolog bibliography (44 entries) has no other stress/prosody title. the JWAL issue listing was confirmed by download. Recommended new-record coding: contrastive (lexical) stress with penultimate default, in a tone language; source Hürlimann & Pike 1985 p. 59. updated at

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive: by default it falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, but some words have final stress (e.g. ca'gaa 'white', par'kuo 'millet') and some trisyllables have initial stress (e.g. 'kaacere 'grasshopper'); minimal-type contrasts such as ka'laangu 'pottery' vs 'kaalungu 'tear' are cited. The stressed syllable licenses the full four-way tone contrast (H, L, rise, fall) and is the usual site of vowel clusters/long vowels; unstressed syllables carry only H or L.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress described; 'A few words have two stresses' (e.g. 'kaa'gbuono 'goat', 'kaami'laano 'kind of rat'), both marked with the primary-stress sign.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed words, initial-stressed trisyllables, and a few double-stressed words are listed as departures from the penultimate default; vowel clusters occasionally occur in two syllables of one word (jaa'tɔɔ 'big', fii'nuɔnɔ 'medication').
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the word in citation form (nouns with class suffixes, verbs, a few short phrases); data from one speaker (Hema Pierre), Niangoloko/Banfora area. The language is tonal: Pike analyses four contrastive tones with the full set only under stress; Lauber's fuller SIL phonology (ms. 1979-80, ed. 2006, co-corrected by Hürlimann) analyses the same facts with two tonemes and word-level tone schemes and never invokes stress, so the 'stress' here is one analyst's (Pike's) culminativity analysis rather than a consensus.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Cerma ('Cerman' in the paper's spelling; autonym cèrmá, people cìràmbá, French 'gouin', Prost's 'kirma') as spoken around Niangoloko and Banfora, SW Burkina Faso, from one speaker (Hema Pierre); no dialect named (Lauber notes three dialects per Hook et al. 1977). Glottocode cerm1238, ISO cme; not the closely related Turka/Curama (turk1309/tuz).

new_statements.quote: For the most part, stress occurs on the next to the last syllable of a word, as in: 'yáángá 'truth' 'cáŋgà 'squash' 'gbǎgá 'bitter' cí'lááŋó 'parrot' jí'gáŋgá 'knife' pò'tótó 'long' bàbá'láŋó 'bad'. There is, however, contrastive placement of stress. For example: 'cíílùŋgù 'heritage' vs cí'lááŋó 'parrot'; ká'lááŋgú 'pottery' vs 'káálúŋgú 'tear'. Stress may occur on the last syllable, as in: cà'gáá 'white' ... pàr'kùɔ 'millet' ... Stress may occur on the first of three syllables. 'kààcèré 'grasshopper' ... 'dìílòŋó 'God, heaven, rain'. A few words have two stresses: 'kàà'gbúòŋò 'goat'
new_statements.citation: Hürlimann, Ruth & Eunice V. Pike. 1985. A note on tone and stress in Cerman. Journal of West African Languages 15(2): 56-60.
new_statements.reading: Cerma has lexically contrastive stress placement coexisting with a four-way tone contrast: penultimate is the default, but final, antepenultimate (first of three) and doubly-stressed words are attested, with minimal pairs by stress position. Stress correlates with vowel-cluster (long) syllables and licenses the full tone inventory (glides only on stressed syllables). Coding suggestion for a new record: 'contrastive/lexical (unpredictable) stress, penultimate default; tone language'. Caveats: five-page note, one speaker, SIL 1985; the fuller Lauber phonology (which Hürlimann herself corrected) analyzes the same facts as tone only and never mentions stress, so the stress-vs-tone interpretation is not independently corroborated.

sources.note: Both tone (H, L, upglide, downglide) and stress placement are contrastive. Stress is mostly on the penultimate syllable of the word, but may fall on the final syllable or on the first of three syllables; a few words have two stresses. Only H and L occur on unstressed syllables; vowel clusters (long/diverse VV) mostly occur only once per word, on the stressed syllable (pp. 56, 59).

sources.quote: p. 23: "Il semble que l'on ait ce redoublement de la consonne après une voyelle brève accentuée. Au contraire après une voyelle longue accentuée, ou après une voyelle non accentuée, la consonne est simple." p. 20: "On a en outre parfois ə, atténuation de l'une ou l'autre voyelle se trouvant en position non accentuée" [EN: It seems this doubling of the consonant occurs after a short stressed vowel. Conversely after a long stressed vowel, or after an unstressed vowel, the consonant is single. / One also sometimes has ə, a weakening of one or the other vowel found in unstressed position.]
sources.note: Presupposes a stressed/unstressed vowel distinction (class-suffix consonant gemination after a short stressed vowel; vowel reduction in unstressed position) but never states where stress falls; no stress marks in the transcriptions of the excerpt. Only the phonology chapter (pp. 19-25) is held by the project; the rest of the 55-page sketch was not seen.
